claims.text: Government can influence business location, production and relationships between firms to pursue employment, development, environmental protection and fair competition. General tools include planning conditions, infrastructure, information, incentives and rules against harmful conduct. Explain why a problem needs attention and how the selected tool changes decisions. A location grant can reduce a site’s cost but cannot supply missing skills or customers by itself. Production standards can protect others but require implementation. Competition measures can address harmful agreements or market power without implying that every large firm is abusive.

claims.text: Government can assist regional development, small firms and exports through grants, subsidies, tax allowances, low-interest loans, cheap or serviced premises, infrastructure, advice, training and information about markets. claims.text: Trade barriers can include tariffs, quotas, embargoes, administrative obstacles and incompatible requirements, while transport, language and payment difficulties can also impede trade. A tariff is a tax on imports; a quota limits quantity; an embargo prohibits specified trade. A tariff can protect a local producer by raising an imported rival’s price, but can also raise input or consumer costs. A quota is not another percentage tax. Describe a barrier’s mechanism and affected parties rather than assume protection benefits everyone.

claims.text: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. Read its direction before calculating: if one foreign unit equals a stated number of N$, multiply foreign units by that N$ amount to convert into N$, or divide N$ by it to obtain foreign units. Show the units and state any assumption about fees. Do not reverse the rate or use a current market rate when a question supplies a hypothetical one. A conversion changes the currency expression, not automatically the underlying value of goods.

claims.text: Namibia is a member of the Southern African Development Community, SADC. Regional cooperation and trading arrangements can improve access to markets, inputs and shared infrastructure. Preferential treatment depends on applicable conditions; regional membership does not mean every product and service faces no barrier. Goods must meet rules-of-origin requirements to qualify for regional preferences. Wider market access can support sales and choice, but Namibian producers also face stronger competition. Benefits depend on competitiveness, logistics, quality and actual demand, while adjustment can impose costs on some firms and workers. Namibia also belongs to the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) with South Africa, Botswana, Lesotho and Eswatini: goods move between members largely free of customs duties, and members charge a common tariff on imports from outside. SADC is a wider regional community; the two organisations are not interchangeable.
